findings.message: A different agent (Claude) checked the work in a separate headless process.

The feature file has 48 scenarios covering all 20 Rules, and most of them are sound. However, the R/G/R ledger does not match the feature: its R19 section has 17 scenario entries, but the feature has 12 R19 scenarios. There are five ledger-only scenarios, each with recorded RED/GREEN proof, that the feature does not contain. That gives 53 ledger entries against 48 feature scenarios. The work log claims the counts match at 48/48, which is no longer true. Several of these orphans describe externally meaningful approval-ledger and configuration behavior. That is exactly the pattern the ticket previously returned to Scenario Gate to fix.

Feature/ledger lineage mismatch under R19. test-definitions.md records RED/GREEN/REFACTOR proof for five scenarios that do not exist in features/approve-coherent-implementation-plans.feature: 'Malformed approval configuration fails closed', 'Implementation Planning exits through the canonical approval boundary', 'A stale fencing generation cannot commit authority', 'The latest serialized decision controls phase and retry identity', and 'Embedded decision markers remain authority-inert'. Trigger: a reviewer or coverage check that reads the ledger sees 53 proven entries, while the accepted behavior contract has 48 scenarios. Consequence: (a) the packet claims proven acceptance behavior that the accepted scenarios do not define. Fail-closed handling of malformed configuration and the canonical phase-exit boundary are user-visible outcomes with no accepted Given/When/Then. (b) The work log's claim that the counts reconcile at 48/48 is false. (c) This repeats the defect from the 2026-09-10T22:23 entry, where ledger concurrency, fencing, and idempotency behavior was added without accepted scenarios. Fix: either add each externally meaningful outcome as an R19 scenario (malformed config fails closed, the canonical exit boundary, inert extension markers that look like decisions), or move internal guards (stale fencing generation, the latest-decision selector) out of this acceptance ledger into lower-level tests. Then reconcile the counts and re-review.

R20 does not cover the parent's non-convergence stop. Parent TBU1.R28 requires every repair pass to materially change the plan or its review basis, and requires Safeword to stop with the remaining findings and their owner instead of re-sending unchanged bytes for review. The child Rule wording leaves out this clause, and no R20 scenario covers an unchanged-bytes re-review. Either add a scenario where the bytes stay unchanged and Safeword stops naming the remaining findings and owner, or record an explicit skip that names the owning sibling.

The Killer Demo scenario under R20 feeds a fixed sequence of deterministic reviewer results, then asserts that all three defects appear together and that approval binds to the corrected bytes. It does not show that the gaps were filled 'through the proper decision owners', which is part of the parent Plan-repair Payoff. Consider asserting which owner resolved each defect, for example that the agent repaired the data owner while the user supplied an authority decision. Alternatively, note this limit as a skip in the spec's Killer Demo line.

Order safety is handled well. The R11 multi-blocker receipt asserts 'without requiring an order', and the R19 concurrency and retry scenarios assert the settled ledger end-state rather than the order of writes.

R7 path admission is discriminating. Each row is a single concrete path, and together they separate an exact file from sibling, nested, non-dated, resolved-outside and outside-directory near misses, so a constant-allow or constant-deny implementation fails.

Scope boundaries hold. R10, R6 and R18 reject execution mechanics (test commands, migration commands, instrumentation) rather than asserting them. R19 approach currency explicitly limits itself to human-approval binding and leaves review-record invalidation to sibling 5F5ZZA, as out_of_scope requires. R14's fixture-minted authority limit is recorded in the ledger.

I found no blocking errors. Each of the 17 Rules has scenarios, and the ledger has a matching entry for all 37 scenarios. Every positive outcome has a negative counterpart that tells them apart. All scenarios are tagged for the Safeword CLI surface, and the other affected surfaces have explicit skips. The two @demo scenarios match the Killer Demo slices this child inherits: the continuation from an accepted plan to the first RED step, and implementation-time replanning. No scenario asserts behavior that out_of_scope excludes. The R14 rows reject claims that Execution Plan approval means implementation, verification, release approval, or merge authority, which matches the exclusion. The scenarios use 5F5ZZA provenance results as inputs and do not implement that mechanism. The warnings below cover inherited parent clauses that no scenario checks, the fact that live scenarios depend on a model's judgment, and inconsistencies in the ledger and work log.

Parent TBU2.R1 allows Execution Planning to start only when the optional human gate in TBU1.R16 is satisfied (when enabled) or recorded as pending on a nonblocking headless surface. The R1 outline has no row for an enabled but unsatisfied human gate, so an implementation could ignore the gate and still pass every R1 row. Child R1's wording leaves the gate out, and TBU1.R16 may belong to a sibling ticket. If this child is responsible for enforcing the gate at the transition, add one blocked row and one headless pending-but-proceeds row. Otherwise, record a skip that names the owner.

Parent TBU2.R17 and the Killer Demo 'Implementation replan' both require renewing an enabled human approval, or recording it as pending on a nonblocking headless surface, before the dependent Execution Plan is refreshed. The R17 design-change row asserts only fresh reviews of both plans. Nothing would fail if a replan resumed work using the previous human approval. Add the renewed-approval outcome to the design-change row, or record which sibling owns it.

Parent TBU2.R11 says that changing canonical contract bytes invalidates that phase's reviews and every review downstream of it. R16's invalidation outline has no contract-byte row. R3 and the R12/R13 identity outlines show that mismatched copies block approval. They do not show that an existing approved review becomes stale after the contract changes. Consider adding a 'canonical contract bytes' row to R16.

The feature file's header says live failures 'are not retried'. However, the work log entry for R10 (2026-09-19T21:26:06) records a retry of the timed-out 'all-decisions-unchanged' case, and that retry produced the 51/51 result. A timeout is arguably not a verdict failure, but the header should say whether timeouts may be retried. Otherwise the live evidence contradicts the feature's stated proof policy.

The @live scenarios (R2, R4, R6, R8, R10, R13, R15, part of R12) depend on a real reviewer model's judgment and are deterministic only through the retained admission matrix. The header correctly treats the corpus checks as supporting evidence only. Make sure CI's installed-CLI runs still exercise the gate's response to both an approving and a rejecting reviewer for each live Rule. Otherwise a reviewer that always approves would only show up in opt-in live runs.

Ledger hygiene: the R6 entry 'Decision specificity controls semantic approval' and the R12 entry 'Delivery evidence uses the canonical checklist taxonomy' each have three RED lines, and the extra lines only correct the reference text. In the R12 entry, RED is a manual or code-inspection skip for characterization of existing behavior. Collapse each to a single authoritative RED line, and for R12 cite the automated characterization receipt rather than code inspection.

R13 'The Execution Plan maps delivery obligations into owned review units' comes close to restating its Given: the Given sets up full dependency-ordered mapping, and the Then mostly confirms ownership. It still passes the vacuous-pass test because 'A complete-looking task list cannot leave delivery obligations unowned' discriminates. Still, the Given should say explicitly that every obligation is assigned to a slice, so the positive case clearly mirrors the rejection.

The R1 provenance outline checks the reported independence level in both directions: the permitted fallback is not reported as independent review, and independent review is not reported as a fallback. A constant label cannot pass both rows.

In the R9 and R16 outlines, ordinary Delivery Checklist progress keeps coding authorized while a change to a Required proof makes the Execution Plan stale. Together these pin the boundary of the normalized fingerprint exactly, and they are consistent with each other.
In the R3 outline, the row with a matching version label but a missing check proves that a version label alone cannot satisfy the identity check, as TBU4.R10 requires.

Each of the five Rules (R1–R5) has a positive scenario and a rejection scenario. Every dimension partition is covered and the surface tags agree with spec.md. The Killer Demo skip is explicit, and out_of_scope is readable and not crossed. The installed-dispatch scenario checks the exact contract digest and the R1–R5 clauses, so it fails if a clause is dropped. I found no blocking defects. There are four non-blocking issues: Then steps that may only repeat a hand-authored corpus plan, a gap in where semantic outcomes are proven, file-count reviewability is never rejected, and the commit-order evidence in the R/G/R ledger can't be checked.

Given-echo risk in the R1 outline 'Contribution shape produces an explicit slicing decision' and the R4 outline 'Conceptual scope determines reviewable slicing'. Their Then steps say 'the plan records …'. The plan is authored content, so if the proof is a corpus fixture plan that already contains one or several PRs with explanations, the assertion passes whether or not the contract or reviewer does anything. Fix: assert what the feature produces, for example 'the CLI-dispatched semantic review approves the plan's recorded single-PR decision with its rationale', so that removing the contract clause changes the result. The sibling rejection scenarios limit but do not remove this risk.

Proof-boundary gap. The feature header says semantic outcomes are exercised by the conformance corpus and a live reviewer matrix, while the normally collected tests guard only 'its exact corpus or CLI boundary'. For every 'semantic review is denied …' Then step, the CI check could pass on corpus structure even if the reviewer no longer denies. Only 'Installed review dispatch carries the canonical slicing contract' is fully deterministic and discriminating. Fix: in the manifest or the implementation plan, state which live-matrix run proves each semantic denial and how often it runs, so a regression in reviewer judgment is caught by a named check.

R4 and the dimensions table cover 'line or file count used as the only criterion', but the rejection scenario 'Line count alone cannot justify a slicing decision' covers line count only. A reviewer that rejects line-count-only justification but accepts file-count-only justification would pass every scenario. Fix: add a row for file count, for example by turning the scenario into an outline over 'line-count threshold' and 'file-count threshold'.

The R/G/R ledger in test-definitions.md can't be checked from this packet. Several REFACTOR hashes match another scenario's GREEN hash: f6e67f8ad is GREEN for the R1 outline and REFACTOR for many others, and 1c4d56d07 is REFACTOR for the R1 outline but GREEN for the dispatch scenario. ee9ce897b is both the dispatch scenario's REFACTOR and the feature-level cross-scenario refactor. If 1c4d56d07 comes before f6e67f8ad in history, the R1 outline's REFACTOR would be recorded before its GREEN. Confirm the order against git history.

Things that look good: 'Installed review dispatch carries the canonical slicing contract' replaces only the external reviewer process with a deterministic recorder and checks the content digest plus the R1–R5 clauses. The R2 and R5 rejection outlines vary one dimension (the missing slice element and the unassigned obligation) and keep the same outcome shape. 'A formally complete slice cannot leave a design decision to its implementer' covers the gap where a slice is structurally complete but semantically unresolved. The R3 scenarios cover both a safe ordering and an unsafe intermediate merge.

Scope and inheritance checks: no scenario covers reviewer assignment, SLAs, WIP limits, or GitHub merge-policy behavior. The line-count rejection is consistent with the out_of_scope exclusion. The Killer Demo has an explicit skip inherited from parent 82T411. Non-CLI hosts are explicitly deferred to YCFFNC in M2, which matches the M1 non-goal. NTB recovery wording is assigned to K3EBHB.

I found no blocking errors, so the verdict is approve, with five warnings. All seven Rules have at least one scenario that can actually fail, and every scenario runs through the installed CLI. The ticket's out-of-scope items and the parent's M1 non-goals are respected. Agent-host surfaces and the Killer Demo are skipped with stated reasons, and the merge-authority and evidence-upgrade invariants each have a falsifying scenario. The warnings cover: (1) a not-applicable mark with no reason has no rejection scenario; (2) the approval-forgery rejection has no visible denial message; (3) the @live scenario's ledger records passing evidence as RED; (4) the R1 heading in test-definitions is out of date; (5) the R4 small-work outline doesn't state what the CLI reports.

R3 says a not-applicable mark needs a concrete reason, but only one example covers this: the honest-disposition outline row 'records not applicable with a concrete reason', which supplies a reason. The @live rejection covers a different case: work that applies being dismissed. An implementation that accepts a not-applicable mark with a blank or vague reason would still pass every scenario, and that breaks the done_when claim 'marked not applicable with a concrete reason'. Add a rejection scenario (or confirm a lower-level table test exists): a not-applicable mark with no concrete reason is refused and the item stays open.

R6 'Contributor evidence cannot record human approval' only asserts that things stay the same: approval remains pending and readiness is unchanged. A CLI approval command that silently does nothing would pass. That still protects the invariant, but there is no visible refusal, so a non-technical builder gets no explanation (NTB1.R1). Add a plain-language denial that names the authorized human as the required approver.

In test-definitions.md, the @live scenario 'Applicable contributor work cannot be dismissed as not applicable' has two RED rows. Both are skip annotations that describe passing results ('matrix rejected the structurally valid... case', '29-case... matrix passed'). Neither records a failure seen before GREEN, so the RED entries can't show that the test fails without the feature. Record a real failing observation (for example, the public CLI regression failing before 5d0652809), or label these rows as live verification rather than RED.

The @live scenario depends on a live Claude Opus judgment, so it can give different results between runs. Its Then ('names the accepted proof boundary') relies on model output. The work log mentions a paired deterministic public CLI regression. Make that regression the acceptance proof for the Then, and keep the live matrix as supporting evidence.

The R1 heading in test-definitions.md leaves out 'and reports in planning order', so it no longer matches the Rule text in the feature file and spec.md. This drift weakens the link between the ledger and the Rule that requires the ordering scenario. Sync the heading.

In the R4 outline 'The feature checklist contract cannot impose feature artifacts on smaller work', the When says the contract is 'evaluated through the installed CLI' but the Then only asserts that nothing is created. Its positive sibling (a feature's checklist lives in its Execution Plan) does rule out a do-nothing implementation, so the outline isn't vacuous. Still, the CLI should say what it reports for a task or patch, for example that the feature checklist contract does not apply and the TBU3 small-work contract governs. Without that, the user gets no clear outcome.

R1's three scenarios cleanly separate the satisfied, single-missing and ordered multi-missing cases. The satisfied case explicitly asserts that no coding or merge authorization is granted, which checks the deny-only claim.

In the R6 readiness outline, the 'approval recorded but merge authority not granted' row and the readiness-only satisfied verdict both check the out-of-scope 'approving or merging on behalf of an authorized human' and the done_when 'never reports merge approval'.

The R7 outline gives each of the four evidence classes a different outcome. The combined rejection scenario (earlier-revision partial proof) checks that evidence is never silently upgraded, and requires both gaps to be named.

Surface coverage holds: Safeword CLI is the only surface tagged, each agent-host surface is skipped and points to YCFFNC in M2, and the Killer Demo is skipped with a reason that inherits from the supplied parent spec. The 'unreadable Execution Plan' scenario covers the failure lens without regenerating the plan.

The scenario set is mostly coherent. Rule lineage is clean, every outline row forces a different outcome, there are opposing positive and negative cases, all tagged surfaces exist in the surfaces file, and nothing crosses the ticket's out_of_scope list. One blocking defect remains: the scenarios never bind the enabled human design-approval gate. Parent rules TBU2.R1, TBU2.R11 and TBU2.R17 and the inherited Implementation-replan Killer Demo all make that gate load-bearing. The R17 'Fresh review can recover…' outline, in its `enabled` row, also lets an implementation enter Execution Planning without any human approval and still pass. The non-blocking warnings are about ledger honesty and proof-boundary gaps.

The enabled human design-approval gate is never bound to a scenario, and one R17 scenario can pass while the gate is bypassed. Parent TBU2.R1 says Execution Planning may begin only when the TBU1.R16 human gate is satisfied when enabled, or recorded as pending on a headless surface. TBU2.R11 says every change that invalidates the Implementation Plan review also invalidates an enabled human approval. TBU2.R17 and the inherited 'Implementation replan' Killer Demo Payoff require renewing that approval (or recording it pending) after a design-changing decision. No scenario covers any of this: the R1 outline has no row for 'human gate enabled and approval absent'; the R16 outline asserts only that planning reviews go stale; the R17 @demo outline's design-change row asserts only fresh exact-content reviews. The trigger: in 'Fresh review can recover an unchanged approach without inventing human authority', the `enabled` row's Given never says a prior human approval exists for the unchanged bytes. Its Then ('enters Execution Planning without another human decision and any existing approval remains bound…') therefore passes for an implementation that skips the human gate whenever no approval exists. The consequence is that Execution Planning can start without a required human design approval while every scenario passes. Fix: (a) in that outline's Given, state that the enabled row has a human approval bound to the exact unchanged approach; (b) add an R1 row where the gate is enabled and approval is absent, which must block (and a headless row that records it pending); (c) in the R17 design-change row, or an R16 row, assert that an enabled human approval becomes stale and must be renewed or recorded pending before work resumes.

In the ledger (test-definitions.md), 'Repeating approval cannot clear a recorded design repair' and 'Fresh review can recover…' leave RED/GREEN/REFACTOR unchecked and only add a free-text 'Proof:' note. Elsewhere this ledger records characterization as checked rows with a `skip: <reason>`. While the ticket is in verify, unchecked rows either block closeout or invite a reader to treat them as already satisfied. Record them in the established `skip:` form with the characterization reason and the test locator.

The ledger still lists R9 'Execution Plan currency controls coding authorization' as RED 7cead12f6 → GREEN 153b78709. The X47AWV lineage assessment says 7cead12f6 was committed after 153b78709, and it found nine non-ancestral RED references in total. R6 and R12 have correction notes, but this row and the other non-ancestral rows do not, so the ledger still asserts a test-first sequence that did not happen. Add correction notes next to each affected row; the history guard requires keeping the original rows.

There is a proof-boundary mismatch on R12 'Delivery evidence uses the canonical checklist taxonomy'. The scenario's When says 'through the installed Safeword CLI', but the ledger's own correction note says the only named automated proof (delivery-checklist-cli.test.ts) mocks review-job lookup/start and proves handler behavior, not installed wiring. The installed path could break while this check still passes. Name a real-subprocess test as this scenario's proof, or narrow the scenario's boundary claim.

The R10 outline's Then ('approval is blocked with the omitted obligation named until it has dependency-ordered work and a completion signal') puts a recovery condition inside an assertion that runs after a single When. The 'until …' clause cannot be observed in this scenario. Assert the blocked verdict and the named obligation; the opposing case is already covered by 'Complete obligation mapping permits semantic approval'.

The @live scenarios rely on a real model reviewer, which is inherently non-deterministic. The header comment correctly says verdict failures are not retried away. Make sure the deterministic CI path for those scenarios still exercises the installed CLI against the content-bound admission artifact, and label any live-only verdict evidence as prior-revision when the corpus or contract bytes change.

Surface coverage is consistent: every scenario carries @surface.safeword-cli, and the spec gives each other affected host an explicit skip that names YCFFNC/M2. No scenario crosses the ticket's out_of_scope list: the 5F5ZZA provenance mechanics are used only as validated inputs, and R14 actively rejects claims of implementation, verification, release or merge.

The Killer Demo is carried correctly by two scenarios: the R2 @demo scenario (accepted plan → reviewed Execution Plan → named RED recorded before any production edit) and the R17 @demo outline (design-changing versus sequencing-only replan, with prior proof preserved and not promoted to a higher currency class). Both match the child's share of the demo, apart from the human-approval gap raised above.

The scenario set is mostly strong. It traces R1–R7 cleanly, gives most happy paths a rejection pair, and orders a collection only where the spec guarantees the order (planning order). It stays inside out_of_scope: it doesn't discover repository policy, hardcode Arcade terms, add a third artifact, or approve or merge on a human's behalf. The surface and Killer Demo skips are explicit and readable from the parent spec that was supplied. One blocking defect remains. The R4 small-work outline asserts only that no artifacts are created, so a do-nothing command passes it. So does a broken command that imposes feature artifacts on a task or patch by demanding them instead of creating them. The warnings cover gaps in the R6 ownership-dependency outcome, the proof boundary of the live R3 scenario, and how the "installed CLI" claims are mapped to handler-level tests.

R4 Scenario Outline 'The feature checklist contract cannot impose feature artifacts on smaller work' passes vacuously. Its only Then is a non-event: 'no feature Implementation Plan or Execution Plan is created'. A CLI command that does nothing for task and patch inputs passes both rows. So does a concrete broken implementation: one that wrongly treats a task or patch as a feature and denies it with 'missing Execution Plan — create one'. That implementation imposes feature artifacts on small work, which the scenario title says cannot happen, yet it never creates a file, so both rows still pass. The sibling feature scenario does not discriminate, because it only asserts where the checklist is recorded. Fix: make the Then say something falsifiable. For example: the CLI reports that the feature Delivery Checklist contract does not apply to the <small_work_type> and defers to the small-work record; it does not deny or request an Implementation Plan or Execution Plan; and no such artifact is created. This keeps TBU3's checklist behavior out of scope while proving the R4 boundary.

R6 says Safeword reports pending human approvals 'or ownership' as unresolved dependencies. The readiness outline only covers pending approval and merge authority. No row shows readiness reporting a recorded human-owned ownership dependency (from R3) as unresolved. Consider adding a row such as 'every contributor-controlled item is proven and a named human-owned dependency is pending' → 'reports ready for human review with that dependency named as unresolved'.

R6 outline row 5 ('ready for human review with the pending approval named') does not explicitly rule out a merge or approval claim. Only row 6 binds the done_when clause 'never reports merge approval when it has established only contributor or review readiness'. Consider adding 'and no merge authorization' to row 5 as well, so an output that also says 'approved to merge' fails there too.

The @live R3 scenario 'Applicable contributor work cannot be dismissed as not applicable' rests on non-deterministic live model judgment. The ledger correction honestly says no live RED was observed. The deterministic public-CLI counterpart uses a stubbed rejecting reviewer, which proves the CLI handles a rejection, not that a real model will make the rejection (the test-quality assessment says the same). Confirm that the counterpart also asserts the Then clause 'the response names the accepted proof boundary'. Also keep the live matrix receipt tied to the current revision, or label it as earlier-revision evidence under this feature's own R7 taxonomy.

Every non-live scenario claims '…through the installed CLI', and the feature header delegates proof to a Vitest manifest that was not supplied. The supplied assessment notes that delivery-checklist-cli.test.ts calls public handlers but mocks review-job lookup and start, and is not an installed-subprocess test. Make sure each scenario maps to a real CLI entry-point test (prerequisite, unreadable-plan, review-wiring, authorization), not only to the handler-level test. Otherwise a broken real wiring could pass while the scenario's 'installed CLI' claim is false.

R1 requires 'one visible default Delivery Checklist', but no scenario covers a contribution whose Execution Plan has duplicate or conflicting checklists. Consider a rejection scenario, or record a skip: reason if this case belongs to a lower-level parser test.

R1 lists missing prerequisites in an order the Rule itself guarantees ('planning order'), so asserting that order is deterministic rather than flaky. Pairing the satisfied verdict with 'no coding or merge authorization' keeps the boundary handed to 7CAMAD visible.

R3's two rejection scenarios (contributor work mislabeled as a human handoff, and applicable work mislabeled as not applicable) together with the unreadable-plan block cover the dishonest-disposition and artifact-integrity partitions in dimensions.md. Each pairs denial with 'the obligation remains open', which a constant-success implementation would fail.

R7's evidence-class outline forces a different recorded claim for each of the four taxonomy classes. Its rejection scenario covers the combined case (earlier-revision and partial), naming both gaps, which directly binds the done_when 'cannot silently become current complete proof'.

I found no blocking defects. I checked each selector's expected test count against the test file. The R17 routing selector matches exactly 8 it.each rows. The 'Implementation Plan review state' selector matches 13 admission tests plus the headless test, for 14 in total. The provenance selector matches 13. The repair-recovery matrix tests both outcomes. If the approach changed and human approval is required, the matrix requires a fresh terminal decision and expects 2 decision events. If the approach bytes are unchanged, it reuses the earlier decision and checks that no new decision event is written. In both cases, the old review receipt is refused before a fresh review. The retained-proof check includes a positive control showing that an accidental rerun would be detected. An unrelated ticket's approval is shown not to clear the recorded repair. When the adapter's count assertion fails, the error code is a string, which still produces a non-zero exitCode, so a miscount cannot report success. The remaining issues are about clarity and coverage only.

In plan-design-approval.test.ts, the first routing row ('the order of independent build tasks changed' → plan-execution) sets `changedApproach: true`. That flag only has an effect on the plan-implementation branch (approveRepairedImplementation), so for this row it does nothing. The test name is generated with %j, so the reported configuration claims a changed approach that was never exercised. Set it to false or leave it out for execution-only rows so the matrix label matches the behavior.

In the changed-approach rows, approveRepairedImplementation changes the plan by calling `.replace('## Architecture applicability', …)` and never checks that the replacement happened. If writeImplementationRoleInputs or convertToCurrentPlanning ever stop writing that heading, the 'changed approach' rows quietly become unchanged-approach rows. The human-gate case would then fail with a confusing message, and the no-gate cases would pass without testing what their names say. Assert that revisedImplementationPlan differs from the original whenever changedApproach is true.

The unchanged-approach recovery rows (changedApproach: false) only use native, current-contract tickets. That matches the current policy, because legacy tickets must convert, and converting changes the bytes. If unchanged-byte recovery is ever claimed for converted legacy tickets, it has no proof here.

The adapter in turn-decisions-into-startable-work.steps.ts fixes expected counts such as 8, 13 and 14 against regex `-t` selectors that also match the describe-block name. Any new test added inside 'Implementation Plan review admission controls Execution Planning' changes two scenario counts at once. Adding a test fails loudly rather than giving a false pass, but the selectors are brittle. Consider naming the tests explicitly, or recording the selected test IDs alongside the counts.

The staleDiscovery step depends on review-job staleness: editing impl-plan.md, which was a review --context file, stops the plan-execution review from being treated as a current changes_requested discovery. plan-approval.ts does not show this coupling directly, but the test does prove it through the real CLI. It would help to note in the test that the stale-context path is what is being proven.
